Nelson Mandela

Politics & Reconciliation · South Africa · 1918–2013

2 min readWhere it is contestedUpdated 19 September 2026
On this pageWhere it is contestedThe definitive biographyReads across to

He entered prison an angry young revolutionary and emerged an elder statesman whose greatest act was refusing the revenge his people had every reason to take.

If you keep one line

Refusing revenge can be the strongest move on the board — forgiveness, wielded as statecraft.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

Mandela spent twenty-seven years in prison. Eighteen of those were on Robben Island, breaking rocks. He was there for leading the armed wing of the struggle against apartheid, South Africa's system of legalized racial domination.

Released in 1990, he negotiated with the regime that had jailed him and steered a country widely expected to collapse into race war toward a peaceful, democratic transition. In 1994 he was elected its first Black president in the nation's first fully free vote. Then he served a single term and stepped down — a rarity among liberation heroes. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission he supported chose acknowledgment over retribution.

His enduring power lies in that discipline of forgiveness wielded as political strategy. It is proof that moral authority can be a form of statecraft, and that even the deepest injustice can sometimes be answered without perpetuating it.

01Where it is contested

Long Walk to Freedom is an autobiography, and its acknowledgements say how it was built. Mandela began it secretly on Robben Island in 1974; the copy he kept was confiscated, and a smuggled one survived. He finished it after his 1990 release with Richard Stengel, credited there with editing the early chapters and writing the later ones. It is a document of the transition as much as a record of a life. Read Sampson alongside it for the independent account.

02The definitive biography

Long Walk to FreedomNelson Mandela · 1994

Mandela's own autobiography, drafted secretly in prison, is the indispensable account — intimate, restrained, and revealing of the discipline behind the icon. For an independent scholarly view, Anthony Sampson's authorized Mandela (1999) is the standard biography.
